questions.problem:
Given that $X∼{χ}^{2}(6),$ what is $P(X<4)$ expressed as an integral?

*Hint: The probability density function ${χ}^{2}(k)$ is given by*

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{2}^{k/2}Γ(\frac{k}{2})}{x}^{k/2-1}{e}^{-x/2}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A chi-square random variable $X∼{χ}^{2}(k)$ with $k$ degrees of freedom has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{2}^{k/2}Γ(\frac{k}{2})}{x}^{k/2-1}{e}^{-x/2}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $X∼{χ}^{2}(6).$ So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8Γ(3)}{x}^{2}{e}^{-x/2}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Recalling that $Γ(n)=(n-1)!$ for any natural number $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
Γ(3)=2!=2.
$$

So, the probability distribution becomes

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}{e}^{-x/2}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we express $P(X<4)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<4) & ={\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}{e}^{-x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{16}{\int }_{0}^{4}{x}^{2}{e}^{-x/2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Finding a Probability Involving Sums of Squared Standard Normal Variables
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$ for $1\leq i \leq k$ are independent normal random variables, then the sum

$$
Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\cdots + Z_{k}^2
$$

follows a $\chi^2(k)$ distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom.

So, in our case, we have

$$
Y = Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\cdots + Z_{10}^2 \sim \chi^2(10).
$$

First, we express the given probability in the form $P(Y\geq y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le y) & =1-P(Y\ge y) \\ 0.99 & =1-P(Y\ge y) \\ P(Y\ge y) & =0.01\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we wish to find the value $y$ such that $P(Y\geq y) = 0.01$ This can be found from the given table:

| $k \setminus p$ | $0.010$ | $0.050$ | $0.100$ | $0.150$ | $0.200$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $8$ | $\,20.090\,$ | $\,15.507\,$ | $\,13.362\,$ | $\,12.027\,$ | $\,11.030\,$ |
| $9$ | $\,21.666\,$ | $\,16.919\,$ | $\,14.684\,$ | $\,13.288\,$ | $\,12.242\,$ |
| $10$ | $\,\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}23.209}\,$ | $\,18.307\,$ | $\,15.987\,$ | $\,14.534\,$ | $\,13.442\,$ |

So, we have

$$
P(Y\geq 23.209) = 0.01
$$

which means

$$
P(Y\leq 23.209) = 0.99.
$$

Therefore, the value $y$ that satisfies $P(Y\leq y) = 0.99$ is $y=\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}23.209}.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
**The chi-square distribution** with $k$ **degrees of freedom**, denoted $\chi^2(k)$, is the distribution of a random variable that is the sum of the squares of $k$ independent standard normal random variables. 

Thus, if $Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_k$ are mutually independent, where $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$, then

$$
Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\ldots+Z_k^2\sim  \chi^2(k).
$$

It can be shown that $X \sim \chi^2(k)$ has the following probability density function:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14254576/assets/6a46942ee5d42c721fb23905e49a67d28c2916eecc234e86734263c599df49fc.svg)

Note that $\Gamma$ is the gamma function.

The diagram below shows $f(x)$ for various degrees of freedom $k.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14254576/assets/cecc3fc82e618f5b5f91e61c4dcab6c1d38b970af20f0ae2baf929b0ce9cdbb3.png)

The chi-square distribution is widely used in inferential statistics. In particular, it is used in **goodness of fit** tests, where experimental data is compared against a hypothesized theoretical model. You will learn more about the applications of the chi-square distribution in future lessons.

tutorials.name: Working With a Percentage Points Table
tutorials.problem:
Let $X\sim\chi^2(3).$ Suppose we wish to know the specific value $x$ such that 

$$
P(X\geq x) = 0.05.
$$

Here, $\alpha = 0.05$ is sometimes called the **significance level**. The required probability is represented by the shaded region below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14254576/assets/34551dd57f17cfb0bdd3bebd2d09c907615f3d936e4b5d69083517d17c1f779f.png)

We often resort to percentage points tables to look up our desired values rather than computing these probabilities by hand (which would be very difficult). 

Some percentage points for the $\chi^2(3)$ distribution are given below. Each cell in the table gives a value $x$ such that $P(X\geq x) = p$ for a particular value of $p.$

| $k \setminus p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $3$ | $\,6.251\,$ | $\,7.815\,$ | $\,9.348\,$ | $\,11.345\,$ | $\,12.838\,$ |

From the table, we have

$$
P(X \geq 7.815) = 0.05.
$$

Therefore, $x = 7.815.$
